content: Calcium oxide (CaO), also known as burnt lime, quicklime, or simply lime, is a chemical compound that appears as a white, caustic, and alkaline crystalline solid. Commercially available lime often contains impurities such as magnesium oxide, silicon oxide, aluminum oxide, and iron oxide. Calcium oxide is typically produced through the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate (CaCO3), commonly found in limestone, in a process known as calcination. This process involves heating the limestone to temperatures exceeding 825°C in a lime kiln, which results in the release of carbon dioxide (CO2) and the formation of calcium oxide. The reaction is reversible, as calcium oxide readily absorbs carbon dioxide from the air upon cooling, eventually converting back into calcium carbonate over time. The calcination of limestone is one of the earliest chemical reactions discovered by humans and was known in prehistoric times. Historically, quicklime was used as a disinfectant, often in the form of a 10% solution called milk of lime. However, its use was limited by its tendency to decompose rapidly when exposed to air and moisture, necessitating the use of freshly prepared quicklime. When calcium oxide reacts with water, it forms calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2), also known as hydrated or slaked lime. This reaction is highly exothermic and produces heat. Hydrated lime is widely used in construction, particularly in mortar and plaster, where it accelerates hardening and improves adhesion. It is also employed in the production of glass and in the metallurgical industry, where it reacts with silicates to remove impurities as slag during the production of steel, magnesium, aluminum, and other metals. In water and sewage treatment, calcium oxide is used to reduce acidity, soften water, act as a flocculant, and remove impurities such as phosphates. In the paper industry, it is utilized to dissolve lignin, as a coagulant, and in bleaching processes. In agriculture, it is applied to acidic soils to improve their quality. Additionally, calcium oxide plays a role in pollution control, particularly in gas scrubbers for desulfurizing waste gases and treating liquid effluents. Historically, quicklime has been used in the burial of bodies in open graves to mask the odor of decomposition. In forensic science, it has been employed to reveal fingerprints. Calcium oxide also serves as a refractory material and a dehydrating agent, and it is used in the purification of citric acid, glucose, and dyes, as well as in the absorption of carbon dioxide. It finds applications in pottery, paints, and the food industry. During epidemics, plagues, and disasters, quicklime has been used to disintegrate bodies to prevent the spread of disease. Calcium oxide is a critical component in the nixtamalization process, which is used to produce corn hominy and masa or tortilla dough. It is an inexpensive substance that generates significant heat energy during its hydration reaction. For example, one liter of water reacts with approximately 3.1 kg of calcium oxide to produce calcium hydroxide and release 3.54 GJ of energy. This exothermic reaction can be harnessed as a portable heat source, such as in self-heating food containers. The reverse reaction, in which calcium hydroxide is heated to regenerate calcium oxide, is also possible. Globally, the annual production of lime is approximately 130 million metric tons. The United States and China are the largest producers, each contributing around 20 million metric tons per year.
